stem: In \(\triangle ABC\) point D on side BC is such that DC = 6, BC = 15. Find \(A(\triangle ABD) : A(\triangle ABC)\) and \(A(\triangle ABD) : A(\triangle ADC)\).
solution:
Point A is common vertex of \(\triangle ABD\), \(\triangle ADC\) and \(\triangle ABC\) and their bases are collinear. Hence, heights of these three triangles are equal.

BC = 15, DC = 6 \(\therefore\) BD = BC \(-\) DC = 15 \(-\) 6 = 9

\(\frac{A(\triangle ABD)}{A(\triangle ABC)} = \frac{BD}{BC}\) .......... heights equal, hence areas proportional to bases.

\(= \frac{9}{15} = \frac{3}{5}\)

\(\frac{A(\triangle ABD)}{A(\triangle ADC)} = \frac{BD}{DC}\) .......... heights equal, hence areas proportional to bases.

\(= \frac{9}{6} = \frac{3}{2}\)

ref: Ratio of areas of two triangles SolvedEx.3
subtopic: Ratio of Areas of Two Triangles
stem: \(\square\) ABCD is a parallelogram. P is any point on side BC. Find two pairs of triangles with equal areas.
solution:
\(\square\) ABCD is a parallelogram.

\(\therefore\) AD \(\parallel\) BC and AB \(\parallel\) DC

Consider \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle BDC\).

Both the triangles are drawn in two parallel lines. Hence the distance between the two parallel lines is the height of both triangles.

In \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle BDC\), common base is BC and heights are equal.

Hence, \(A(\triangle ABC) = A(\triangle BDC)\)

In \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle ABD\), AB is common base and heights are equal.

\(\therefore A(\triangle ABC) = A(\triangle ABD)\)
note: The stem introduces a point P on side BC, but the book's own printed solution never uses P — the two pairs it gives are (ABC, BDC) and (ABC, ABD).

subtopic: Ratio of Areas of Two Triangles
stem:
In adjoining figure 1.12, in \(\triangle ABC\), point D is on side AC. If AC = 16, DC = 9 and BP \(\perp\) AC, then find the following ratios.

(i) \(\frac{A(\triangle ABD)}{A(\triangle ABC)}\)

(ii) \(\frac{A(\triangle BDC)}{A(\triangle ABC)}\)

(iii) \(\frac{A(\triangle ABD)}{A(\triangle BDC)}\)
solution:
In \(\triangle ABC\) point P and D are on side AC, hence B is common vertex of \(\triangle ABD\), \(\triangle BDC\), \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle APB\) and their sides AD, DC, AC and AP are collinear. Heights of all the triangles are equal. Hence, areas of these triangles are proportional to their bases. AC = 16, DC = 9

\(\therefore\) AD = 16 \(-\) 9 = 7

\(\therefore \frac{A(\triangle ABD)}{A(\triangle ABC)} = \frac{AD}{AC} = \frac{7}{16}\) ........ triangles having equal heights

\(\frac{A(\triangle BDC)}{A(\triangle ABC)} = \frac{DC}{AC} = \frac{9}{16}\) ........ triangles having equal heights

\(\frac{A(\triangle ABD)}{A(\triangle BDC)} = \frac{AD}{DC} = \frac{7}{9}\) ........ triangles having equal heights

subtopic: Basic Proportionality Theorem
stem: In \(\triangle ABC\), DE \(\parallel\) BC. If DB = 5.4 cm, AD = 1.8 cm, EC = 7.2 cm then find AE.
solution:
In \(\triangle ABC\), DE \(\parallel\) BC

\(\therefore \frac{AD}{DB} = \frac{AE}{EC}\) ..... Basic proportionality theorem

\(\therefore \frac{1.8}{5.4} = \frac{AE}{7.2}\)

\(\therefore AE \times 5.4 = 1.8 \times 7.2\)

\(\therefore AE = \frac{1.8 \times 7.2}{5.4} = 2.4\)

AE = 2.4 cm

stem:
Can we say that the two triangles in figure 1.52 similar, according to information given? If yes, by which test?

(Fig. 1.52 prints XY = 14 and YZ = 20 in \(\triangle XYZ\), MN = 21 and NP = 30 in \(\triangle MNP\), and marks \(\angle Z \cong \angle P\).)
solution:
\(\triangle XYZ\) and \(\triangle MNP\),

\(\frac{XY}{MN} = \frac{14}{21} = \frac{2}{3}\),

\(\frac{YZ}{NP} = \frac{20}{30} = \frac{2}{3}\)

It is given that \(\angle Z \cong \angle P\).

But \(\angle Z\) and \(\angle P\) are not included angles by sides which are in proportion.

\(\therefore \triangle XYZ\) and \(\triangle MNP\) can not be said to be similar.

subtopic: Tests of Similarity of Triangles
stem: Diagonals of a quadrilateral ABCD intersect in point Q. If 2QA = QC, 2QB = QD, then prove that DC = 2AB.
solution:
Given : 2QA = QC, 2QB = QD

To prove : CD = 2AB

Proof : 2QA = QC \(\therefore \frac{QA}{QC} = \frac{1}{2}\) .......... (I)

2QB = QD \(\therefore \frac{QB}{QD} = \frac{1}{2}\) .......... (II)

\(\therefore \frac{QA}{QC} = \frac{QB}{QD}\) .......... from (I) and (II)

In \(\triangle AQB\) and \(\triangle CQD\),

\(\frac{QA}{QC} = \frac{QB}{QD}\) .......... proved

\(\angle AQB \cong \angle DQC\) .......... opposite angles

\(\therefore \triangle AQB \sim \triangle CQD\) .......... (SAS test of similarity)

\(\therefore \frac{AQ}{CQ} = \frac{QB}{QD} = \frac{AB}{CD}\) .......... corresponding sides are proportional

But \(\frac{AQ}{CQ} = \frac{1}{2}\) \(\therefore \frac{AB}{CD} = \frac{1}{2}\)

\(\therefore 2AB = CD\)

subtopic: Theorem of Areas of Similar Triangles
stem: \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR\), \(A(\triangle ABC) = 16\), \(A(\triangle PQP) = 25\), then find the value of ratio \(\frac{AB}{PQ}\).
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the stem prints \(A(\triangle PQP) = 25\); the third vertex should be R, and the book's own solution reads it as \(A(\triangle PQR) = 25\).]

\(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR\)

\(\therefore \frac{A(\triangle ABC)}{A(\triangle PQR)} = \frac{AB^2}{PQ^2}\) .......... theorem of areas of similar triangles

\(\therefore \frac{16}{25} = \frac{AB^2}{PQ^2}\) \(\therefore \frac{AB}{PQ} = \frac{4}{5}\) .......... taking square roots
note: Book misprint, verified on the page at 3x zoom: the stem prints 'A (\(\triangle\)PQP) = 25' where it must be \(\triangle\)PQR. The P is unambiguous (closed bowl, no leg) beside the R of '\(\triangle\) PQR' earlier on the same line. Transcribed as printed.

ref: Theorem of areas of similar triangles SolvedEx.2
subtopic: Theorem of Areas of Similar Triangles
stem: Ratio of corresponging sides of two similar triangles is 2:5, If the area of the small triangle is 64 sq.cm. then what is the area of the bigger triangle?
solution:
Assume that \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR\).

\(\triangle ABC\) is smaller and \(\triangle PQR\) is bigger triangle.

\(\therefore \frac{A(\triangle ABC)}{A(\triangle PQR)} = \frac{(2)^2}{(5)^2} = \frac{4}{25}\) .......... ratio of areas of similar triangles

\(\therefore \frac{64}{A(\triangle PQR)} = \frac{4}{25}\)

\(4 \times A(\triangle PQR) = 64 \times 25\)

\(A(\triangle PQR) = \frac{64 \times 25}{4} = 400\)

\(\therefore\) area of bigger triangle = 400 sq.cm.

subtopic: Property of an Angle Bisector of a Triangle
stem:
In \(\triangle PQR\) seg PM is a median. Angle bisectors of \(\angle PMQ\) and \(\angle PMR\) intersect side PQ and side PR in points X and Y respectively. Prove that XY \(\parallel\) QR.

Complete the proof by filling in the boxes.

In \(\triangle PMQ\), ray MX is bisector of \(\angle PMQ\).

\(\therefore \frac{\text{(blank)}}{\text{(blank)}} = \frac{\text{(blank)}}{\text{(blank)}}\) .......... (I) theorem of angle bisector.

In \(\triangle PMR\), ray MY is bisector of \(\angle PMR\).

\(\therefore \frac{\text{(blank)}}{\text{(blank)}} = \frac{\text{(blank)}}{\text{(blank)}}\) .......... (II) theorem of angle bisector.

But \(\frac{MP}{MQ} = \frac{MP}{MR}\) .......... M is the midpoint QR, hence MQ = MR.

\(\therefore \frac{PX}{XQ} = \frac{PY}{YR}\)

\(\therefore\) XY \(\parallel\) QR .......... converse of basic proportionality theorem.
